purpose: Answer what the 2026 Middle East energy shock actually cost India, in the voice of someone who has read PPAC's monthly import tables, the Comptroller General's accounts and the World Bank's June 2026 Global Economic Prospects, and noticed that they tell a stranger story together than any of them does alone. Open on the fact, not the framing: on 27 February 2026 a conflict effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, traffic through it fell about 97% within a fortnight, and Brent went from $71 to a $138 peak. Then pose the puzzle plainly. India buys about 88% of the crude it burns and sits in the most Gulf-exposed region on earth, yet the World Bank RAISED its growth forecast in the same edition that cut 112 of 170 others. Do not resolve that puzzle with the words 'resilience' or 'decoupling'. Resolve it mechanically, in this order. First, the exposure is a gradient, not a number: over nine-tenths of India's LPG comes from the Gulf against under half its crude. Second, that gradient predicted exactly what happened. India kept importing almost the identical volume of crude, 81.9 million tonnes against 81.5 a year earlier, because Russia and the United States sell barrels that never touch the strait, and it paid $22.8 billion more for them. LPG had no such substitute and imports nearly halved. Third, the cost did not reach the pump: retail petrol inflation was 7.5% in July against an 81% rise in the landed crude price. Fourth, find where it went instead. Union excise, which after GST is almost entirely fuel tax, fell 22% in April-June; the urea subsidy rose 68%; and the petroleum subsidy line did not move at all, because India held prices down by giving up revenue rather than by paying a subsidy. Land the verdict as a qualified answer: the shock was large and it landed, but it landed on the import bill and the exchequer instead of the household, and one large piece of the bill cannot be seen yet. Be scrupulous that the World Bank upgrade is against January's forecast and not against last year, and that India still decelerates from 7.7% to 6.6%. Never use an em dash. Never write that India was immune, escaped, or decoupled. Never claim the current account widened.
tension: Every instinct says an economy that imports 88% of its oil, from the most exposed region on earth, cannot take a doubling of the oil price without pain. India took it and its growth forecast went up. The resolution is not that India is stronger than it looks. It is that the country had quietly rebuilt its crude supply around Russia and never did the same for the cooking gas in ninety million kitchens, and that the pain it did take was moved off household bills and onto the government's books, where nobody has to look at it.
requiredConcepts: The conflict began on 27 February 2026, the last market day before it being 27 February. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell roughly 97% between February and March 2026 and had not recovered by 24 May, when the World Bank's series ends. The World Bank publishes this without naming a unit, so it must be described as a percentage change or an index, never in tonnes.
Brent crude peaked at $138.2 a barrel in April 2026, from about $63 in December 2025. Monthly averages: $71.1 in February, $103.7 in March, $120.4 in April, $83.4 by July.

India's REALISED crude import price, which is what actually left the country, peaked at $118.6 a barrel in MAY 2026, two months after the reference basket peaked, because cargoes are priced weeks before they land. It was $65.6 in February. That is a rise of about 81%. Always quote this series and never the Indian basket for 'what India paid'.

PPAC's March 2026 Indian basket price of $113.49 is not usable. The basket is a blend of Brent Dated and the Oman/Dubai average; March Brent averaged $103.7 and Dubai Fateh $91.9, so no weighting of the two can produce it. Do not state this figure.

India imported 81.9 million tonnes of crude between April and July 2026 against 81.5 million tonnes a year earlier, a rise of under half a percent, and paid $63.4 billion against $40.6 billion. The extra cost is about $22.8 billion over four months, a rise of 56%. In rupees the bill went from about 3.48 lakh crore to about 5.94 lakh crore.

In 2025, before the shock, 91.5% of India's LPG import value came from the seven Gulf economies, against 60.8% of its LNG, 47.9% of its crude, 41.7% of its DAP fertiliser, 27.2% of its refined fuels and 20.9% of its urea. Gulf here means Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and excludes Oman because its ports sit outside the strait.

Russia supplied about 32.7% of India's crude import value in 2025 and the United States about 5.7%. Iraq was 18.2%, Saudi Arabia 14.6% and the UAE 10.8%. This diversification after 2022 is why crude volumes held.

India's LPG imports fell from 7.08 million tonnes in April-July 2025 to 3.70 million tonnes in April-July 2026, a fall of 47.7%, while the price paid per tonne rose about 59% from $533.9 in February to a peak of $851.5 in May. These are imports, not consumption; domestic production and stocks filled part of the gap.

In July 2026, year-on-year consumer price inflation was 4.44% headline, 7.5% for petrol, 8.4% for diesel, 6.2% for CNG and 5.0% for LPG cylinders. MOSPI rebased the CPI to 2024 in January 2026, so these are not continuous with the older 2012-base series, which stops in December 2025.

Across April to June 2026 against a year earlier: union excise collections fell 22.4% (from about 55,605 crore to 43,149 crore), the urea subsidy rose 68.2% (31,523 to 53,034 crore), the nutrient-based fertiliser subsidy rose 22.5%, and the petroleum subsidy stayed near nil at 282 crore. April posts as a near-zero or negative month for excise in these accounts every year, so only April-June totals are comparable.

Customs collections rose 36.1% over the same window, so excise and customs together were roughly flat at plus 2.9%. Customs covers all imports and India levies little basic customs duty on crude, so this rise must NOT be attributed to oil.

The World Bank's June 2026 Global Economic Prospects cut global growth for 2026 to 2.5%, the weakest since the pandemic. Of 170 emerging-market entries carrying a revision, 112 were cut, 43 raised and 15 unchanged.

India's forecast growth is 7.7% for FY2025-26, 6.6% for FY2026-27 and 7.2% for FY2027-28. The FY2026-27 figure is 0.1 percentage points ABOVE the January 2026 forecast of 6.5%, and FY2027-28 is 0.6 points above. India still decelerates by 1.1 points. The World Bank attributes the offset to lower US tariffs after the Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs, new free trade agreements with the EU and the UK, a GST rate cut and a reduction in fuel taxes.
India's quarterly growth ran 6.8% in 2025Q2, 8.3% in 2025Q3, 8.0% in 2025Q4 and an estimated 7.8% in 2026Q1, the quarter the conflict began in its final month.

South Asia is the EMDE region where the largest share of economies source over 30% of their oil from the Middle East, at 50%, and gas, at 33%. This counts economies and not volumes, and South Asia has six economies in the sample, so 50% means three of six. It is not an India-specific statistic.

The current-account impact CANNOT be stated. RBI publishes the balance of payments about a quarter in arrears. The latest published quarter, January to March 2026, contains only one month of the conflict and recorded a surplus of about $7.1 billion. The first full shock quarter was unpublished as of late August 2026. Any claim about the current account must be flagged as inferred from monthly trade, never as measured.
requiredSections: What actually happened at the end of February?
Why does one strait matter so much to India?
So why did India's crude keep arriving?
What did the same barrels end up costing?
Why did cooking gas behave so differently?
Why didn't any of this show up at the pump?
Then why did the World Bank raise India's forecast?
styleExample:
## So why did India's crude keep arriving?

Because India had already stopped depending on the strait for it, without ever framing the change that way.

Go back to 2021 and the Gulf supplied most of India's crude. Then Europe stopped buying Russian oil, Russia started discounting it, and Indian refiners spent three years rebuilding their supplier list around a barrel that arrives via the Suez Canal or the Cape, and never passes Hormuz at all. By 2025 Russia was about a third of India's crude import bill and the United States another twentieth.

None of that was done as energy security policy. It was done because the oil was cheap. But when the strait closed in March 2026, the effect was the same as if it had been: India had a second set of suppliers already under contract, already tested, already shipping. Volumes barely moved. What moved was the price, because a world short of Gulf crude bids up every other barrel too, discount or not.

The test of that explanation is what happened to the one product India never diversified.
